Remembered faith and personal support answer shame about a chained teacher

Paul writes as a prisoner (verse 8), and many have left him (verse 15). Shame is the danger the chapter names three times. Verse 8 tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony or of Paul. Verse 12 says Paul is not ashamed, for he knows whom he trusted. Verse 16 praises Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of the chain. The ground for courage comes just before, in verse 7. God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control.
Patient correction must accompany careful teaching and shared endurance

Verse 23 tells Timothy to refuse foolish questions, because they breed quarrels. Verse 24 gives the rule for the Lord’s servant: he must not quarrel. Three qualities replace quarreling: gentle toward all, able to teach, and patient. Verse 25 keeps correction in place but sets its tone: gentleness. The reason is hope for the opponent. God may give them repentance and knowledge of the truth. Verse 26 says they may yet escape the devil’s snare.
Received Scripture equips conduct amid deceptive displays of religion

Verse 13 says deceivers will grow worse. Verse 14 tells Timothy to stay with what he has learned. Verse 15 says the holy Scriptures can make him wise for salvation. Verse 16 lists four uses: teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. Verse 17 gives the purpose of all four. The person who belongs to God becomes complete. He is equipped “for every good work,” so the end of the list is action.
Urgent teaching and ordinary needs stand together near the speaker's expected departure

Verse 1 sets the charge before God and Christ the judge. Verse 2 gives five commands in a row. The first is to announce the word. The second is to be ready in season and out of season. Reprove, rebuke, and exhort follow, with patience and teaching. Verses 3–4 explain the urgency: hearers will turn from the truth to fables. Verse 6 adds another reason: Paul’s own departure is near.
